(CNN) -- Madagascar's military handed over the reins of the island nation to opposition leader Andry Rajoelina on Wednesday, ending a two-month long political crisis -- but apparently creating a constitutional one. Andry Rajoelina is six years too young to be Madagascar's president under its constitution. Rajoelina, a former disc jockey turned mayor of Madagascar's capital, declared himself president of a transitional government and his supporters pledged to hold elections in two years. But Rajoelina, at 34, is six years too young to be president, according to the country's constitution. Also, the constitution says the head of parliament's upper house must call elections within two months if something happens to the president. Madagascar's former president, Marc Ravalomanana, ceded power to his military Tuesday after insisting over the weekend that he would remain in control. Analysts think Ravalomanana had little choice but to step down once he had lost much of the army's support. The African Union had warned that any power transfer aided by the military would amount to a coup d' etat. The Union has since removed any mention of a coup in its official communique and called on the transitional government to "comply scrupulously with the provisions of the constitution of Madagascar on interim arrangements." Monja Roindefo, the opposition-appointed prime minister, vigorously defended the week's developments on the island, located off the southeastern coast of Africa. "Well, we would like to define what is a coup," he told CNN on Wednesday. "A coup is a group of people or persons who takes the power on behalf of sovereignty, on behalf of the people ... when the representative democracy doesn't work anymore." "As you know, as stated, in the African Union charter, the people have the right to defend itself from an oppression or a dictatorship in Africa," he added. Roindefo said the new government will hold elections but has given itself two years to clean up the process.  Watch more from iReporters and Twitterers on the crisis » . "How could you make an election immediately?" he said. "We need to reform the electoral commission. ... So the 24 months that we have given ourselves is to prepare all these types of elections in order to build a genuine democratic country." The African Union also asked that all steps be taken to ensure the safety of the former president. The opposition leader had called for Ravalomanana's arrest, accusing him of corruption, financial mismanagement and dictatorship. Ravalomanana was first elected in 2001 and won a second term in 2006. To many Malagasy, he represented a new breed of politician -- a self-made millionaire, a no-nonsense business leader. But Ravalomanana maintained his business empire while in office and it was unclear to many where his business interests ended and his political leadership began. His recent purchase of a $60 million airplane further stoked public discontent. Opposition leader Rajoelina was quick to seize on the sentiments and made fiery appeals to the country's impoverished masses. The country was plunged into political instability in January after thousands of people took to the streets to protest rising food prices and what they perceived as autocratic behavior by Ravalomanana. The protests soon degenerated into rioting and looting, and left about 100 people dead.  Watch more on president's resignation » . Soon after, Rajoelina declared that he was in charge of the country. He gave Ravalomanana until early February to step down. The president responded by firing Rajoelina as mayor of the capital, inciting the latter's supporters to once again descend on the streets. More deadly violence followed. Clashes spread to most provincial capitals and other cities across the country, with homes and businesses looted and burned, the U.S. State Department reported. CNN's David McKenzie contributed to this report.

(CNN) — Madagascar’s military handed control of the island nation to opposition leader Andry Rajoelina on Wednesday, ending a two-month political crisis while apparently creating a constitutional one.

Rajoelina, a former disc jockey who became mayor of Madagascar’s capital, declared himself president of a transitional government, and his supporters pledged to hold elections within two years. However, at 34, Rajoelina is six years too young to serve as president under the country’s constitution. The constitution also stipulates that if something happens to the president, the head of parliament’s upper house must call elections within two months.

Madagascar’s former president, Marc Ravalomanana, ceded power to the military Tuesday after insisting over the weekend that he would remain in control. Analysts believe Ravalomanana had little choice but to step down once he had lost much of the army’s support.

The African Union had warned that any transfer of power aided by the military would amount to a coup d’état. The organization has since removed any mention of a coup from its official communiqué and called on the transitional government to “comply scrupulously with the provisions of the constitution of Madagascar on interim arrangements.”

Monja Roindefo, the opposition-appointed prime minister, strongly defended the week’s developments on the island, located off the southeastern coast of Africa.

“Well, we would like to define what is a coup,” he told CNN on Wednesday. “A coup is a group of people or persons who takes the power on behalf of sovereignty, on behalf of the people ... when the representative democracy doesn’t work anymore.”

“As you know, as stated, in the African Union charter, the people have the right to defend itself from an oppression or a dictatorship in Africa,” he added.

Roindefo said the new government would hold elections but had given itself two years to reform the process.

“How could you make an election immediately?” he said. “We need to reform the electoral commission. ... So the 24 months that we have given ourselves is to prepare all these types of elections in order to build a genuine democratic country.”

The African Union also called for all necessary measures to ensure the safety of the former president. Rajoelina had previously called for Ravalomanana’s arrest, accusing him of corruption, financial mismanagement and dictatorship.

Ravalomanana was first elected in 2001 and won a second term in 2006. To many Malagasy, he represented a new kind of politician: a self-made millionaire and a decisive business leader. Yet he maintained his business empire while in office, leaving many uncertain where his business interests ended and his political leadership began. His recent purchase of a $60 million airplane further fueled public discontent.

Rajoelina quickly capitalized on those sentiments, making impassioned appeals to the country’s impoverished masses.

Madagascar was plunged into political instability in January after thousands of people took to the streets to protest rising food prices and what they viewed as Ravalomanana’s increasingly autocratic behavior. The protests soon descended into rioting and looting, leaving about 100 people dead.

Soon afterward, Rajoelina declared that he was in charge of the country and gave Ravalomanana until early February to step down. The president responded by dismissing Rajoelina as mayor of the capital, prompting Rajoelina’s supporters to return to the streets.

More deadly violence followed. According to the U.S. State Department, clashes spread to most provincial capitals and other cities across the country, with homes and businesses looted and burned.

CNN’s David McKenzie contributed to this report.

Under Madagascar’s constitution, Rajoelina is not old enough to serve as president: at 34, he falls six years short of the required age. Rajoelina, a former disc jockey who later became mayor of the capital city, announced that he was the president of a transitional administration. His backers said elections would be held in two years.

The constitution also provides that, if the presidency becomes vacant, the leader of parliament’s upper chamber must organize elections within two months.

Former President Marc Ravalomanana handed power to the military on Tuesday, despite having said over the weekend that he intended to remain in office. Analysts said Ravalomanana appeared to have few options after losing the support of much of the army.

The African Union had cautioned that any military-assisted transfer of power would be considered a coup d’état. However, the organization later removed references to a coup from its official statement and urged the transitional authorities to “comply scrupulously with the provisions of the constitution of Madagascar on interim arrangements.”

Monja Roindefo, who was named prime minister by the opposition, strongly defended the events of the week in the island nation, which lies off Africa’s southeastern coast.

“Well, we would like to define what is a coup,” he told CNN on Wednesday. “A coup is a group of people or persons who takes the power on behalf of sovereignty, on behalf of the people ... when the representative democracy doesn't work anymore.”

He added, “As you know, as stated, in the African Union charter, the people have the right to defend itself from an oppression or a dictatorship in Africa.”

Roindefo said the incoming government does plan to organize elections, but that it has allowed itself two years to overhaul the electoral system first.

“How could you make an election immediately?” he said. “We need to reform the electoral commission. ... So the 24 months that we have given ourselves is to prepare all these types of elections in order to build a genuine democratic country.”

The African Union also called for every necessary measure to be taken to protect the safety of the former president.

Rajoelina had demanded Ravalomanana’s arrest, accusing him of corruption, mishandling public finances and ruling like a dictator.

Ravalomanana was first voted into office in 2001 and secured another term in 2006. Many people in Madagascar saw him as a different kind of political leader: a self-made millionaire and a hard-driving businessman. Yet he continued to control his business holdings while president, leaving many unsure where his private commercial interests ended and his role as national leader began. Public anger intensified after he recently bought a $60 million aircraft.

Rajoelina moved quickly to capitalize on that dissatisfaction, delivering impassioned messages aimed at the country’s poor majority.

Madagascar fell into political turmoil in January, when thousands of demonstrators went into the streets to protest increasing food costs and what they viewed as Ravalomanana’s authoritarian conduct. The demonstrations soon turned into riots and looting, leaving about 100 people dead.

Not long afterward, Rajoelina proclaimed that he was running the country. He set an early-February deadline for Ravalomanana to resign. In response, the president dismissed Rajoelina from his post as mayor of the capital, prompting Rajoelina’s supporters to return to the streets.

Further fatal violence followed. According to the U.S. State Department, clashes expanded to most provincial capitals and other cities throughout Madagascar, while homes and businesses were looted and set on fire.

CNN’s David McKenzie contributed to this report.

## Rajoelina Takes Power in Madagascar After Ravalomanana Steps Down, Sparking Coup Debate

**Antananarivo, Madagascar — March 2009** — Madagascar’s months-long political crisis reached a dramatic turning point as President **Marc Ravalomanana** stepped down under intense pressure from opposition protests and a divided military, clearing the way for opposition leader **Andry Rajoelina** to assume power as head of a transitional authority.

The transfer of power has plunged the Indian Ocean island nation into a constitutional and diplomatic controversy, with Rajoelina and his allies insisting the change reflects popular will, while critics at home and abroad describe it as a military-backed coup.

### Ravalomanana resigns amid pressure

Ravalomanana, a wealthy businessman who had led Madagascar since 2002, announced that he was relinquishing power after weeks of escalating unrest. His decision followed mass demonstrations, violent confrontations, and a growing loss of support within sections of the armed forces.

Rather than handing authority directly to Rajoelina, Ravalomanana transferred power to a military directorate. But within hours, the military leadership passed authority to Rajoelina, the former mayor of Antananarivo and Ravalomanana’s most prominent opponent.

Madagascar’s **High Constitutional Court** subsequently endorsed Rajoelina as head of state, giving legal cover to a transition that many international observers still viewed as deeply irregular.

### Rajoelina’s rise

Rajoelina, then 34, had built his political movement around accusations that Ravalomanana had become authoritarian, corrupt, and disconnected from ordinary Malagasy citizens. He had been dismissed as mayor of the capital earlier in the crisis after his opposition movement gained momentum.

The confrontation intensified in February 2009 when security forces opened fire on opposition supporters near the presidential palace in Antananarivo, killing and wounding protesters. The incident hardened opposition demands for Ravalomanana’s departure and weakened the president’s position.

Rajoelina declared himself leader of a transitional authority and promised new elections, though the timetable and constitutional basis for the transition remained contested. Under Madagascar’s constitution, the presidency had a minimum age requirement that Rajoelina did not meet, further fueling debate over the legality of his takeover.

### Monja Roindefo defends the transition

Rajoelina appointed **Monja Roindefo**, a longtime opposition figure, as prime minister of the transitional government. Roindefo rejected allegations that the transfer of power amounted to a coup.

“This is not a coup d’état,” Roindefo told reporters, defending the new administration as the result of a popular uprising against a discredited government. He argued that the transition reflected “the will of the people” after institutions had failed to resolve the crisis.

Roindefo also suggested that the opposition movement had acted because normal democratic channels had broken down. “When representative democracy no longer works, the people must make themselves heard,” he said in remarks defending the legitimacy of Rajoelina’s authority.

He pledged that the transitional government would organize elections and restore constitutional order, saying the new leadership did not intend to remain in power indefinitely.

### Was it a coup?

The central question surrounding the crisis is whether Rajoelina’s accession was a popular revolution, a constitutional transition, or a military-backed coup.

Supporters of Rajoelina argue that Ravalomanana had lost legitimacy through repression, alleged abuses of power, and refusal to heed popular demands. They point to the scale of opposition demonstrations, the president’s resignation, and the Constitutional Court’s approval of the transfer as evidence that the transition had domestic legitimacy.

Critics counter that Ravalomanana resigned only after military pressure and that the armed forces effectively determined the outcome by handing authority to Rajoelina. They also note that the constitutional line of succession was bypassed, and that Rajoelina was too young to qualify for the presidency under the existing constitution.

The **African Union** condemned the takeover as unconstitutional and suspended Madagascar from participation. Regional bodies, including the **Southern African Development Community**, also rejected the transfer of power and called for a return to constitutional rule. Several Western governments expressed concern, with some suspending non-humanitarian aid.

International critics described the events as a coup because power changed hands outside normal constitutional procedures and with decisive military involvement. Even though Ravalomanana formally resigned, the circumstances of his departure — mass unrest, army defections, and the military’s role in transferring power — left the new government facing a legitimacy crisis.

### A divided country

The crisis exposed deep political and social divisions in Madagascar. Ravalomanana’s supporters accused Rajoelina of seizing power through street pressure and military backing. Rajoelina’s supporters accused Ravalomanana of turning the state into a vehicle for personal and commercial interests.

The instability threatened Madagascar’s already fragile economy, including its textile industry, tourism sector, and foreign investment. The political uncertainty also raised concerns about poverty, food security, and governance in one of the world’s poorest countries.

### Uncertain transition

Rajoelina’s transitional authority promised elections, constitutional reforms, and national reconciliation. But the path forward remained unclear, with international recognition limited and pressure mounting for a negotiated settlement involving all major political factions.

For many outside observers, the crisis became a test case for how to distinguish between a popular uprising and an unconstitutional seizure of power. For Madagascar, it marked the beginning of a prolonged transition whose legitimacy would remain contested long after Ravalomanana’s departure.

**ANTANANARIVO, Madagascar — March 2009 (CNN)** — Madagascar plunged deeper into constitutional uncertainty this week after President Marc Ravalomanana ceded power to the military and opposition leader Andry Rajoelina declared himself head of a transitional government, capping weeks of violent unrest and a bitter power struggle in the Indian Ocean island nation.

Ravalomanana, who had led Madagascar since 2002, announced Tuesday that he was transferring authority to a military directorate, saying the move was intended to prevent further bloodshed after a standoff with opposition forces and mutinous soldiers. But within hours, senior military figures handed power to Rajoelina, the 34-year-old former mayor of the capital, Antananarivo, who has led mass demonstrations demanding the president’s resignation.

Rajoelina quickly declared that he was in charge of a “High Transitional Authority” and promised new elections within two years. His supporters celebrated in the streets of Antananarivo, while international organizations warned that the transfer of power bore the hallmarks of an unconstitutional coup.

The crisis has left Madagascar — one of the world’s poorest countries despite rich reserves of minerals, timber and biodiversity — facing political isolation, economic uncertainty and the prospect of renewed unrest.

## A rapid transfer of power

Ravalomanana’s decision to step down followed days of mounting pressure from opposition supporters and segments of the armed forces. A group of soldiers had earlier mutinied and refused orders to suppress demonstrations, shifting the balance of power away from the president.

In a statement broadcast to the nation, Ravalomanana said he was handing authority to a military council led by Vice Adm. Hyppolite Ramaroson. The council, however, almost immediately transferred power to Rajoelina.

Madagascar’s High Constitutional Court later recognized Rajoelina as the country’s transitional leader, giving his takeover a degree of domestic legal cover. But critics noted that the constitution requires a president to be at least 40 years old — six years older than Rajoelina — and contains no clear mechanism allowing the military to hand power to an opposition figure.

Rajoelina has argued that Ravalomanana lost legitimacy through authoritarian rule, misuse of state resources and the violent suppression of protests.

“We are establishing a transition,” Rajoelina told supporters, pledging to restore democracy and organize elections. “The people have won.”

## International condemnation

The African Union, the Southern African Development Community and other international actors reacted sharply, warning that the events in Antananarivo amounted to an unconstitutional change of government.

The African Union condemned the transfer and signaled that Madagascar could face suspension unless constitutional order is restored. SADC, of which Madagascar is a member, also rejected the takeover and called for a return to legality.

Western governments, including the United States and France, expressed concern and urged calm, dialogue and elections. Donors are watching closely: Madagascar relies heavily on foreign assistance, and political instability could threaten aid flows, trade preferences and investment.

Diplomats said the central question is whether Rajoelina’s administration can persuade the international community that it is a temporary authority leading to credible elections — or whether it will be treated as a coup government.

## Weeks of deadly unrest

The crisis began in January after Rajoelina, then mayor of Antananarivo, accused Ravalomanana of ruling like a dictator and demanded his resignation. The government shut down a television station owned by Rajoelina after it aired an interview with former President Didier Ratsiraka, a longtime rival of Ravalomanana.

Rajoelina’s rallies drew tens of thousands of people to the capital’s main square. Protests turned violent, with looting and fires reported in Antananarivo and other cities.

The bloodiest episode came on February 7, when presidential guards opened fire on opposition demonstrators marching toward the presidential palace. Dozens were killed or wounded, galvanizing anger against Ravalomanana and deepening divisions inside the military.

Ravalomanana later dismissed Rajoelina as mayor, but the move failed to weaken the opposition movement. Instead, Rajoelina increasingly presented himself as the leader of a national uprising.

## The military’s decisive role

The armed forces proved decisive in the final days of the standoff. Soldiers at a key military camp outside the capital mutinied, saying they would no longer take orders to fire on civilians. Their defection emboldened opposition supporters and undermined Ravalomanana’s grip on power.

By Monday, pro-Rajoelina forces had taken control of the presidential palace in central Antananarivo, although Ravalomanana was not there at the time. The president remained at another residence outside the capital, protected by loyalists but increasingly isolated.

Analysts say the military’s intervention created the appearance of a civilian-led transition while effectively removing the elected president under pressure.

“The army did not simply stand aside,” one regional observer said. “It became the arbiter of political power.”

## Ravalomanana’s fall

Ravalomanana, a wealthy businessman and founder of the Tiko dairy empire, came to power after a disputed 2001 election and a prolonged confrontation with then-President Ratsiraka. He was initially praised by foreign donors for economic reforms, infrastructure projects and efforts to attract investment.

But his critics accused him of blurring the line between state power and private business, concentrating authority in the presidency and sidelining opponents. Rising frustration over poverty, inequality and perceived corruption fed the opposition movement.

A controversial agreement to lease large amounts of farmland to the South Korean company Daewoo Logistics also fueled public anger, with critics portraying it as a giveaway of national resources. Although the deal’s details remained disputed, it became a symbol of distrust toward Ravalomanana’s government.

## Who is Andry Rajoelina?

Rajoelina, a former disc jockey and advertising entrepreneur, entered politics as mayor of Antananarivo and became one of Ravalomanana’s most visible challengers. Young, media-savvy and populist, he built support among urban residents frustrated by unemployment, rising prices and what they saw as presidential arrogance.

His critics say he lacks national experience and came to power through street pressure and military backing rather than elections. Supporters say he gave voice to public anger and forced out a president who had become increasingly authoritarian.

Rajoelina’s transitional authority has said it will rewrite parts of the political system and prepare for elections, but has not yet presented a detailed timetable acceptable to all sides.

## Uncertain road ahead

The immediate challenge for Madagascar is whether rival factions can avoid further violence. Ravalomanana’s supporters remain a significant force, particularly in parts of the countryside, and it is unclear whether they will accept Rajoelina’s leadership.

The economy is also vulnerable. Madagascar’s textile industry, mining projects and tourism sector all depend on stability and foreign confidence. Political sanctions or aid suspensions could hit hard in a country where most people live on less than a few dollars a day.

Humanitarian organizations warn that prolonged instability could worsen poverty and undermine health and education programs.

For now, Rajoelina controls the capital and has the backing of key military leaders. But his authority remains contested abroad and constitutionally disputed at home.

Madagascar’s crisis, once a political rivalry between a president and a dismissed mayor, has become a test of whether power on the island will be determined by elections, courts and constitutional rules — or by street mobilization backed by soldiers.
